decks.title: Cash Book — Part 1: Subsidiary Books and the Simple Cash Book
goals: Explain why the journal is divided into subsidiary books, state their advantages and name the books
Prepare a simple (single column) cash book, balance it and explain why its balance can never be a credit balance
Post the lines of a cash book to the ledger accounts using To and By and the correct side

slides.heading: The cash book: subsidiary books and the simple cash book
slides.body_md: Part 1 — why the **journal is divided**, the **subsidiary books**, and the **simple cash book**: recording, balancing and posting.

visual.alt: Route map of Part 1: a transaction is first recorded in a subsidiary book such as the cash book, then posted to the ledger accounts, which feed the trial balance
visual.caption: Part 1 at a glance

slides.narration: Welcome to the chapter on the cash book. A busy firm cannot write every transaction in one journal, so the journal is divided into subsidiary books, and the cash book is the most important of them. In this part we see why the journal is divided, then build a simple cash book for an imagined hardware shop, balance it and post it to the ledger.

slides.heading: Why the journal is divided
slides.body_md: As a firm grows, hundreds of similar transactions arrive every day. One journal cannot hold them without delay and confusion, so it is **sub-divided** into **subsidiary books**, each for one class of transactions.

rows: Several clerks, each with a book
Totals of a period are posted together
Open the book of its class
Check the book of that class

visual.alt: Table comparing one journal for everything with subsidiary books on who writes, posting, looking for a transaction and finding an error

slides.narration: In a small firm one journal is enough. As business grows, the same kinds of transactions repeat all day, cash received, goods bought, goods sold. Writing all of them in a single journal is slow and confusing. So the journal is divided into subsidiary books, and each book takes one class of transaction. This is called the sub division of the journal.

slides.heading: Advantages of subsidiary books
slides.body_md: Dividing the journal by class of transaction gives these gains.

rows: Different clerks write different books at the same time
A clerk who writes one kind of entry becomes quick and accurate
Totals are posted instead of every item
All transactions of one class are together
A mistake is searched for in one book only
Each clerk is answerable for his own book

visual.alt: Table of six advantages of subsidiary books: division of work, specialisation, saving of time and labour, easy reference, errors located quickly and internal check

slides.narration: There are six main advantages. Work is divided among several clerks. Each clerk becomes a specialist in one kind of entry. Time and labour are saved because totals are posted instead of every item. Information is easy to find. Errors are traced to one book. And each clerk answers for his own book, which is an internal check on fraud.

slides.heading: The subsidiary books at a glance
slides.body_md: The **cash book** is taught in this chapter. The other books are only **named** here; Chapter 6 teaches them.

rows: All receipts and payments of cash and through the bank
Small cash payments on the imprest system
Bills receivable and bills payable books
Bills of exchange received and accepted
Entries that belong to no other book

visual.alt: Table of the subsidiary books: cash book, purchases book, sales book, purchases returns book, sales returns book, petty cash book, bills books and journal proper, with what each records and where it is taught
visual.caption: The subsidiary books at a glance

slides.narration: Here are the subsidiary books. The cash book records every receipt and payment of cash and through the bank. Then come the purchases book, the sales book, and the purchases returns and sales returns books. The petty cash book holds small payments. Bills books are named for completeness. The journal proper takes entries that fit no other book. Chapter six teaches the books other than the cash book.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: which book first records it?
slides.body_md: Udaya Pens, an imagined firm, has six transactions. Decide the **subsidiary book** in which each is **first recorded**.
bullets: Cash received or paid always starts in the **cash book**.
Credit purchases and credit sales go to the **purchases** and **sales** books.
Returns have their own books; depreciation goes to the **journal proper**.

rows: Sold goods on credit to Gita Traders for ₹14,000
Bought goods on credit from Rao Papers for ₹9,500
Sent back goods worth ₹1,200 to Rao Papers

visual.alt: Table assigning six transactions to their subsidiary books: credit sale to the sales book, cash payment to the cash book, credit purchase to the purchases book, purchase return to the purchases returns book, sales return to the sales returns book and depreciation to the journal proper
visual.caption: Each transaction goes to one book

slides.narration: Look at the nature of each transaction. A credit sale goes to the sales book. Salaries paid in cash go to the cash book. Goods bought on credit go to the purchases book. Goods sent back to the supplier go to the purchases returns book, and goods sent back by a customer to the sales returns book. Depreciation is an adjustment, so it goes to the journal proper.

slides.heading: Quick check: the first book
slides.body_md: Decide whether cash is involved.
slides.narration: Ask whether any cash passes in the transaction. If it does, the first record is in the cash book. If not, think of credit purchases, credit sales or returns.

slides.heading: The cash book: two roles in one book
slides.body_md: The **cash book** records every receipt and payment of cash, and with the triple column form, bank items as well. It plays two roles at once.

rows: Every receipt and payment of cash is written in it first, in date order
No cash entry is made in the journal
It is balanced like an account: receipts on the debit side, payments on the credit side
No separate Cash A/c is kept in the ledger

visual.alt: Table of the two roles of the cash book: a book of original entry for cash transactions and, because it is balanced like an account, the Cash A/c itself

slides.narration: The cash book does two jobs. First, it is a book of original entry for cash. Every receipt and payment is written in it first, in date order, and not in the journal. Second, it is balanced like a ledger account, with receipts on the debit side and payments on the credit side. So it is also the cash account, and the ledger does not keep another one.

slides.heading: Format of the simple cash book
slides.body_md: A **simple cash book** has one money column on each side. The **debit side** holds the receipts and the **credit side** the payments. Each side has date, particulars, ledger folio and amount.

visual.alt: Format of a simple cash book of Kundan Hardware, an imagined shop: the debit side for receipts and the credit side for payments, each with date, particulars, ledger folio and an amount column, the opening balance first on the debit side
visual.caption: Single column cash book: first lines of June 2027

slides.narration: The simple cash book is drawn with two sides. The left side is the debit side for receipts. The right side is the credit side for payments. Each side has a date, a particulars column, a ledger folio column and one amount column. The first line on the debit side is the cash in hand at the start, written as To Balance brought down.

slides.heading: Rules for recording
slides.body_md: Every line names the **other account** of the transaction. The ledger folio is filled in after the line is **posted**.

rows: Cash sales, cash from a debtor, any receipt
Purchases for cash, expenses, drawings, payment to a creditor
Not posted: it is the Cash A/c itself

visual.alt: Table of the rules of the simple cash book: receipts on the debit side with To and the other account, payments on the credit side with By and the other account, opening cash as To Balance b/d

slides.narration: Follow three rules. Receipts go on the debit side, and the particulars begin with the word To followed by the other account, for example To Sales or To a debtor. Payments go on the credit side with the word By and the other account. Cash already in hand at the start is the first debit line, To Balance brought down.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: recording and balancing
slides.body_md: **Kundan Hardware**, an imagined shop, had cash of ₹18,000 on 1 June 2027. Its cash transactions for June are entered and balanced here. The closing cash is ₹10,200.
bullets: Debit side: opening cash and the receipts add up to ₹37,050.
Credit side: payments of ₹26,850 and the balance c/d of ₹10,200.

visual.alt: Simple cash book of Kundan Hardware for June 2027 after balancing: receipts of thirty seven thousand fifty rupees on the debit side including the opening cash, payments and the balance carried down of ten thousand two hundred rupees on the credit side, with ledger folios and both totals equal
visual.caption: Kundan Hardware, June 2027: simple cash book

slides.narration: Kundan Hardware starts June with rupees eighteen thousand in hand. The receipts, with the opening cash, come to rupees thirty seven thousand fifty. The payments come to rupees twenty six thousand eight hundred fifty. The difference of rupees ten thousand two hundred is written on the credit side as balance carried down, so both sides total rupees thirty seven thousand fifty. It is brought down on the debit side on the first of July.

slides.heading: Balancing the cash book
slides.body_md: The cash book is balanced at the end of each period, as a ledger account is. The balance is **always a debit balance** or nil.

nodes.label: Write it as Balance c/d on the credit side
Write the equal total on both sides
Bring it down below as Balance b/d

visual.alt: Five steps of balancing a simple cash book: total each side in rough, find the difference, write it as balance carried down on the credit side, write the equal total on both sides and bring the balance down on the debit side
visual.caption: Balancing the cash book

slides.narration: To balance the cash book, total each side in rough. Find the difference. Write it on the credit side as balance carried down, so the two sides become equal. Write the same total on both sides on the same line. Then bring the balance down on the debit side below the totals. That is the cash in hand at the start of the next period.

slides.heading: Quick check: where does the balance go?
slides.body_md: Recall the side of balance c/d and of balance b/d.
slides.narration: The cash in hand is a debit balance, so the carried down line is on the smaller side, which is the credit side, and the brought down line is on the debit side.

slides.heading: Cash can never be a credit balance
slides.body_md: A shop cannot pay out more cash than it holds. If the credit side is larger than the debit side, there is **a mistake in the entries**.

headers: If the credit side is larger
rows: Impossible: payments cannot exceed cash held
Receipt left out or on the wrong side
Cash paid was counted too much
Part of the cash in hand was ignored
Bring it in as To Balance b/d

visual.alt: Table of what a credit balance of cash in a cash book would mean: it is impossible, so the clerk checks for an omitted receipt, a payment entered twice or a forgotten opening balance

slides.narration: Cash paid out can never be more than the cash held plus the cash received. So the debit side of the cash book is never smaller than the credit side. If it seems so, a receipt has been left out or put on the wrong side, a payment has been entered twice or too high, or the opening cash was forgotten. Recheck the entries.

slides.heading: Posting the cash book to the ledger
slides.body_md: The cash book is itself the Cash A/c, so **only the other accounts** are posted. A **receipt** is **credited** to the other account as **By Cash A/c**; a **payment** is **debited** to it as **To Cash A/c**.

visual.alt: Table showing how each line of the simple cash book of Kundan Hardware is posted: every receipt is credited to the other account as By Cash A/c and every payment is debited to the other account as To Cash A/c
visual.caption: Posting the cash book to the ledger

slides.narration: Every line of the cash book is posted to the ledger account named in its particulars. A receipt was a debit in the cash book, so the other account is credited, and the entry reads By Cash. A payment was a credit in the cash book, so the other account is debited, and the entry reads To Cash. No account is opened for cash itself.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: posting a debtor's account
slides.body_md: Anil Rao owed Kundan Hardware ₹10,000 on 1 June 2027, and bought goods worth ₹4,800 on credit on 2 June (entered in the sales book). He paid ₹6,200 in cash on 8 June. Post his account and balance it.
bullets: Opening balance and the credit sale go on the **debit** side.
The cash received goes on the **credit** side, **By Cash A/c**.
The balance is a debit balance of ₹8,600.

rows: 2 Jun To Sales A/c (credit sale, Sales Book)

visual.alt: Account of Anil Rao in the ledger of Kundan Hardware: a debit balance of ten thousand rupees brought down, a credit sale of four thousand eight hundred rupees on the debit side, and the receipt of six thousand two hundred rupees on the credit side as By Cash, leaving a debit balance of eight thousand six hundred rupees
visual.caption: Debtor: Anil Rao A/c

slides.narration: Anil Rao is a debtor, so his account opens with a debit balance of ten thousand rupees. The credit sale of rupees four thousand eight hundred is a further debit. The cash book shows that he paid rupees six thousand two hundred, so his account is credited, and the entry reads By Cash. The credit side is smaller, so a balance of rupees eight thousand six hundred is carried down on it, and he still owes that amount.

slides.heading: Worked example 4: posting a creditor's account
slides.body_md: Kundan Hardware owed Mehta Suppliers ₹9,000 on 1 June 2027 and paid ₹4,200 in cash on 22 June. Post the account and balance it.
bullets: The opening balance of a creditor is on the **credit** side.
A payment in the cash book is posted on the **debit** side, **To Cash A/c**.

visual.alt: Account of Mehta Suppliers in the ledger of Kundan Hardware: a credit balance of nine thousand rupees brought down and a payment of four thousand two hundred rupees on the debit side as To Cash, leaving a credit balance of four thousand eight hundred rupees
visual.caption: Creditor: Mehta Suppliers A/c

slides.narration: Mehta Suppliers is a creditor, so the account opens on the credit side with nine thousand rupees. The cash book shows a payment of rupees four thousand two hundred to the supplier. A payment is a credit in the cash book, so it is a debit here, and the entry reads To Cash. The credit side is larger, so the balance of rupees four thousand eight hundred is carried down on the debit side. The firm still owes it.

slides.heading: Quick check: posting a payment
slides.body_md: Work out the side of the other account.
slides.narration: A payment is on the credit side of the cash book. Then ask which side of the other account must be written, and which word begins the particulars.

slides.heading: Slips to avoid

rows: A receipt entered on the credit side
Receipts on the debit side with To
The balance c/d written on the debit side
The credit side is the smaller side
Balance c/d on the credit side, b/d on the debit side
Keeping a separate Cash A/c as well
The cash book is the cash account
Naming Cash in the cash book particulars
The other account must be named
To Sales A/c, By Rent A/c and so on
Posting a payment to the credit of the expense

visual.alt: Table of five common slips in a simple cash book, why each is wrong and the correct practice

slides.narration: Five slips cost marks. Do not put a receipt on the credit side. Do not write the balance carried down on the debit side. Do not keep a separate cash account as well as the cash book. Do not forget to name the other account in the particulars. And do not post a payment to the credit of an expense, because an expense is always debited.

slides.heading: Summary of Part 1

rows: The journal is divided by class of transaction; the totals are posted to the ledger
Book of original entry and the Cash A/c in one
Receipts on the debit side with To; payments on the credit side with By; name the other account
Cash is never a credit balance; c/d on the credit side, b/d on the debit side
Receipt: credit the other account, By Cash A/c. Payment: debit it, To Cash A/c

visual.alt: Summary table of Part 1: subsidiary books, the cash book, recording, balancing and posting

slides.narration: To sum up. The journal is divided into subsidiary books so that work is shared and totals are posted. The cash book is a book of original entry and the cash account in one. Receipts are debits with To and payments are credits with By. The balance is never a credit. In posting, a receipt credits the other account and a payment debits it.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: Write the **opening cash** as the first debit line, **To Balance b/d**.
Name the **other account** with **To** or **By** on every line.
Balance c/d goes on the **credit** side; show **equal totals** and **b/d** below.
To post, **receipt = credit** the other account, **payment = debit** it.
If your cash balance is a credit, recheck the entries before moving on.
slides.narration: Examiners give marks for entering the opening balance, the receipts, the payments, the balance carried down, the equal totals and the postings. Common slips are putting a receipt on the credit side, forgetting the balance brought down, and naming the wrong account. If cash comes out negative, go back and find the mistake.

decks.title: Cash Book — Part 2: Triple Column Cash Book, Contra Entries and a Fixed Cash Balance
goals: Prepare a triple column cash book with discount, cash and bank columns, using contra entries and treating cheques correctly
Total the discount columns and post them; post individual lines to personal accounts; show a bank overdraft as a credit balance
Maintain a definite cash balance at the end of each day by depositing the excess or withdrawing the shortfall

slides.heading: The triple column cash book
slides.body_md: Part 2 — **discount, cash and bank columns**, **contra entries**, **cheques**, **overdraft** and keeping a **definite cash balance**.

visual.alt: Route map of Part 2: the triple column cash book takes receipts and payments into discount, cash and bank columns, with contra entries and cheques, is balanced and then posted
visual.caption: Part 2 at a glance

slides.narration: In part two the firm has a bank account, and gives and receives discount. The cash book grows a discount column and a bank column on each side, and a new kind of entry appears, the contra entry. We deal with cheques, balancing, the posting of discount, an overdraft at the bank, and keeping a fixed balance of cash, all with imagined firms.

slides.heading: The three money columns
slides.body_md: The **triple column cash book** has a **discount**, a **cash** and a **bank** column on each side. Discount **allowed** is on the debit side and discount **received** on the credit side.

visual.alt: Format of the triple column cash book of Bhavna Electricals, an imagined firm: each side has date, particulars, ledger folio, a discount column, a cash column and a bank column; discount allowed is on the debit side and discount received on the credit side
visual.caption: Three money columns on each side

slides.narration: Each side of the triple column cash book has three money columns. They are discount, cash and bank. On the debit side the discount column holds discount allowed, and on the credit side it holds discount received. The first line shows the opening cash and the opening bank balance. A payment by cheque goes to the bank column, and a payment in notes to the cash column.

slides.heading: Discount allowed and discount received
slides.body_md: A **debtor** who pays early may be **allowed** a discount, a loss for the firm. A **creditor** who is paid early may **allow** the firm a discount, a gain.

rows: Allowed to a debtor who pays early
Received from a creditor who is paid early
At the end of the month
Column totalled; debit Discount Allowed A/c
Column totalled; credit Discount Received A/c

visual.alt: Table comparing discount allowed and discount received on whom it is given to or received from, the column of the cash book, its nature, the posting of the column total and the entry in the personal account

slides.narration: Discount allowed is given to a debtor who pays early. It is a loss, and it stands on the debit side of the cash book. Discount received comes from a creditor whom the firm pays early. It is a gain, and it stands on the credit side. In the personal account of the debtor the discount is a credit, and in that of the creditor it is a debit.

slides.heading: Contra entries
slides.body_md: A **contra entry** is a transaction that affects both the **cash** and the **bank** column, so it appears on **both sides**. It is marked **C** in the folio column and is **not posted**.

rows: Cash deposited into the bank (₹12,000 on 12 Nov)
Cash withdrawn for office use (₹8,000 on 15 Nov)

visual.alt: Table of the two contra entries: a deposit of cash debits the bank column and credits the cash column; a withdrawal for office use debits the cash column and credits the bank column; both are marked C and are not posted
visual.caption: Contra entries appear on both sides

slides.narration: A contra entry moves money between cash and bank inside the same book. When cash is deposited, the bank column is debited and the cash column is credited. When cash is withdrawn for use in the office, the cash column is debited and the bank column is credited. Both lines are marked with the letter C, and neither is posted to a ledger account.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: the first three entries
slides.body_md: **Bhavna Electricals**, an imagined firm, has ₹25,000 in cash and ₹60,000 at the bank on 1 November 2027. It receives a cheque for ₹9,600 from Rohit Jain, after allowing him ₹400 discount, and deposits it. It pays Sumit Traders ₹18,800 by cheque, after discount of ₹1,200.
bullets: Receipt: **To Rohit Jain** with discount allowed and the cheque in the **bank** column.
Payment: **By Sumit Traders** with discount received and the cheque in the **bank** column.

visual.alt: Opening balances of cash and bank, then a receipt from Rohit Jain by cheque with discount allowed of four hundred rupees, then a payment to Sumit Traders by cheque with discount received of one thousand two hundred rupees, balanced on the fifth of November
visual.caption: Bhavna Electricals: the first three entries

slides.narration: The cheque from Rohit Jain was deposited at once, so it goes in the bank column on the debit side, with the discount of rupees four hundred in the discount column beside it. The payment to Sumit Traders is by cheque, so it goes in the bank column on the credit side, with discount received of rupees one thousand two hundred. The cash column is not touched by either.

slides.heading: Quick check: a cheque kept for three days
slides.body_md: Think about where the cheque is until it is paid in.
slides.narration: The cheque was first entered in one column. When it is paid in, it moves to another. Decide which two columns are affected and on which sides.

slides.heading: Cheques: three cases
slides.body_md: The column depends on whether the firm **holds the cheque** or the **bank holds it**.

rows: Cheque received and deposited the same day
Debit side, bank column, against the customer
Cheque received and not deposited the same day
Debit side, cash column, against the customer
Contra entry on the day it is deposited
Credit side, bank column, against the customer

visual.alt: Table of three cheque cases: a cheque deposited the same day goes to the bank column; one kept and deposited later goes first to the cash column and then by a contra entry to the bank column; a dishonoured cheque is credited in the bank column

slides.narration: There are three cases. A cheque deposited on the day it is received goes straight to the bank column on the debit side. A cheque kept in the drawer is treated like cash in hand, so it goes first to the cash column, and a contra entry moves it to the bank column on the day it is deposited. A cheque that is later dishonoured is taken out of the bank column.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: a cheque not deposited the same day
slides.body_md: On 8 November Bhavna Electricals receives a cheque for ₹12,000 from Karan Mehra and keeps it. It is paid into the bank on 12 November and returned unpaid on 21 November.
bullets: 8 Nov: **To Karan Mehra** in the **cash** column.
12 Nov: **contra entry**; bank column debited, cash column credited.
21 Nov: **By Karan Mehra** in the **bank** column.

visual.alt: The cheque of twelve thousand rupees from Karan Mehra: received on the eighth of November and entered in the cash column, paid into the bank on the twelfth by a contra entry, and returned unpaid on the twenty first and credited in the bank column
visual.caption: Karan Mehra's cheque: received, deposited, dishonoured

slides.narration: On the eighth of November the cheque of rupees twelve thousand is entered in the cash column on the debit side. On the twelfth it is paid in, so a contra entry credits the cash column and debits the bank column. On the twenty first the bank returns the cheque, so the bank column is credited against Karan Mehra. The cash and bank columns for this cheque are now both nil.

slides.heading: A dishonoured cheque
slides.body_md: When the bank returns a deposited cheque **unpaid**, the receipt is **cancelled**: the bank column is **credited** and the customer is **debited** again in the ledger.

rows: Credit side, bank column: By Karan Mehra
The bank balance falls by the cheque
Karan Mehra A/c: To Bank A/c on the debit side

visual.alt: Table of the two entries for a dishonoured cheque: a credit in the bank column of the cash book and a debit in the ledger account of the customer, so that he owes the amount again

slides.narration: A dishonoured cheque is as if the money had never arrived. In the cash book the amount is entered on the credit side in the bank column, with the customer named. In the ledger the customer is debited again, so that he is once more a debtor for the cheque. Any further charge by the bank is entered separately as bank charges.

slides.heading: Balancing the triple column cash book
slides.body_md: Cash and bank are **balanced separately**. The **discount columns** are **only totalled**: the two totals are not equal and nothing is carried down.

nodes.label: Total each money column on both sides
Cash c/d on the credit side; bank c/d on the credit side if favourable, on the debit side if overdrawn
Equal totals in cash and bank columns

visual.alt: Five steps of balancing the triple column cash book: total, balance cash and bank separately, carry each down on the proper side, show equal totals in the cash and bank columns and only total the discount columns
visual.caption: Balancing the triple column cash book

slides.narration: Total the cash column and the bank column on each side. Find the balance of each. The cash balance is always carried down on the credit side. The bank balance is carried down on the credit side if it is favourable, and on the debit side if it is an overdraft. The cash and bank totals then agree. The discount columns are only totalled, and not balanced.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: a month of the triple column cash book
slides.body_md: Bhavna Electricals, November 2027: the complete cash book. Closing cash is ₹38,850 and closing bank is ₹29,080. Discount allowed totals ₹550 and discount received ₹1,200.
bullets: Cash column total ₹67,350 and bank column total ₹82,700 on each side.
The deposit of the cheque and the withdrawal for the office are contra entries.

visual.alt: Triple column cash book of Bhavna Electricals for November 2027 after balancing: cash balance of thirty eight thousand eight hundred fifty rupees and bank balance of twenty nine thousand eighty rupees carried down on the credit side, discount allowed of five hundred fifty rupees and discount received of one thousand two hundred rupees totalled and not balanced
visual.caption: Bhavna Electricals, November 2027

slides.narration: For the month, the cash column on each side totals rupees sixty seven thousand three hundred fifty and the bank column rupees eighty two thousand seven hundred. Cash of rupees thirty eight thousand eight hundred fifty and bank balance of rupees twenty nine thousand eighty are carried down on the credit side. The discount columns are not equal. Discount allowed is rupees five hundred fifty and discount received is rupees one thousand two hundred. They are totalled and posted.

slides.heading: Quick check: the bank balance
slides.body_md: Include the contra entry in the bank column only once.
slides.narration: The bank column takes the opening balance, the cheque deposited, the cash deposited, and less the cheque paid. Cash sales do not enter the bank column.

slides.heading: Posting the discount columns
slides.body_md: At the month end the two discount columns are **totalled**. The debit total is posted to the **debit** of **Discount Allowed A/c** and the credit total to the **credit** of **Discount Received A/c**, both as **Sundries as per Cash Book**.

rows: To Sundries as per Cash Book
By Sundries as per Cash Book

visual.alt: Posting of the two discount totals of Bhavna Electricals: Discount Allowed A/c debited with five hundred fifty rupees and Discount Received A/c credited with one thousand two hundred rupees, both as Sundries as per Cash Book
visual.caption: Discount totals are posted, not balanced

slides.narration: The total of the debit discount column, rupees five hundred fifty, is posted to the debit of the Discount Allowed account, as to Sundries as per the cash book. The total of the credit discount column, rupees one thousand two hundred, is posted to the credit of the Discount Received account. Each is posted once. The individual discounts are posted to the personal accounts.

slides.heading: Posting personal accounts: a debtor with discount
slides.body_md: Rohit Jain owed ₹10,000. The cash book shows ₹9,600 by cheque and ₹400 discount, so his account is credited with **both**, By Bank A/c and By Discount Allowed A/c, and closes.

visual.alt: Account of Rohit Jain in the ledger of Bhavna Electricals: debit balance of ten thousand rupees brought down, credited by the bank for nine thousand six hundred rupees and by Discount Allowed for four hundred rupees so that the account closes with no balance
visual.caption: Debtor settled with discount: Rohit Jain A/c

slides.narration: Rohit Jain owed ten thousand rupees. He paid rupees nine thousand six hundred by cheque, and the firm allowed discount of rupees four hundred. His account is credited twice. First by Bank, then by Discount Allowed. The credit side then equals the debit side, so the debtor is settled in full and the account shows no balance.

slides.heading: The bank overdraft
slides.body_md: An **overdraft** is a facility by which the bank lets the firm pay out more than it has deposited. In the cash book it is a **credit balance** of the bank column.

rows: Nature of the bank column balance

sections.heading: 1. Sub-division of the journal: purpose and advantages
sections.body_md:
In a business with many transactions one journal becomes too slow and too crowded. The journal is therefore **sub-divided** into **subsidiary books** (special journals), each recording one class of transactions in its own ruling. Totals of a period are then posted to the ledger.

**Advantages**
- **Division of work:** several clerks write different books together.
- **Specialisation:** each clerk becomes skilled in one class of entry.
- **Saving of time and labour:** totals are posted instead of every item.
- **Easy reference:** all transactions of a class are together.
- **Errors and fraud:** an error is searched for in one book; each clerk is answerable for his own book (internal check).

The subsidiary books are a first stage only. The ledger is still the principal book and the trial balance is still prepared from it.

sections.heading: 3. The simple cash book: format and recording
sections.body_md:
The **cash book** is both a book of original entry for cash and the Cash A/c of the ledger. No separate cash account is kept.

**Format (simple, one column):** a two-sided ruling. The **debit side** holds receipts and the **credit side** payments; each side has date, particulars, ledger folio (L.F.) and an amount.

**Recording:** the opening cash is the first debit line, **To Balance b/d**. Every receipt is entered on the debit side with **To** and the other account; every payment on the credit side with **By** and the other account. The L.F. is filled in after posting.

sections.heading: 4. Balancing the simple cash book and posting it
sections.body_md:
**Balancing:** total each side in rough; the debit side (with opening cash) is the larger. Write the difference on the credit side as **By Balance c/d**; write the equal total on both sides; bring the balance down on the debit side as **To Balance b/d**.

**Cash can never be a credit balance.** A firm cannot pay out more cash than it holds, so a credit balance signals a mistake: a receipt omitted, a payment overstated or entered twice, or the opening cash forgotten.

**Posting:** the cash book is itself the Cash A/c, so only the other accounts are posted. A **receipt** is a debit in the cash book, so the other account is **credited** (**By Cash A/c**). A **payment** is a credit in the cash book, so the other account is **debited** (**To Cash A/c**). Expenses and incomes are posted in the same way. Personal accounts are then balanced.

sections.heading: 5. The triple column cash book and contra entries
sections.body_md:
The **triple column cash book** has three money columns on each side: **discount**, **cash** and **bank**. **Discount allowed** (to debtors, a loss) is in the debit side discount column; **discount received** (from creditors, a gain) is in the credit side discount column.

A **contra entry** is a transaction between the cash and bank columns, so it is entered on **both sides** of the same book and marked **C** in the L.F. column; it is **not posted**.
- **Cash deposited into the bank:** bank column debited (To Cash A/c), cash column credited (By Bank A/c).
- **Cash withdrawn from the bank for office use:** cash column debited (To Bank A/c), bank column credited (By Cash A/c).

Payments and receipts by cheque go to the bank column; bank charges and interest on the bank statement are entered in the bank column on the side they affect.

sections.heading: 6. Cheques, balancing the discount columns and posting
sections.body_md:
**Cheques**
- **Received and deposited the same day:** debit side, bank column, against the customer.
- **Received and not deposited the same day:** debit side, **cash** column, against the customer; when it is deposited, a **contra entry** (bank column debited, cash column credited).
- **Dishonoured** after deposit: **credit** side, **bank** column, against the customer, who is debited again in the ledger.

**Balancing:** cash and bank are balanced separately and their totals agree on both sides; the cash balance c/d is on the credit side. The **discount columns are only totalled** (the two totals differ).

**Posting:** the debit total goes to the **debit of Discount Allowed A/c** and the credit total to the **credit of Discount Received A/c**, as Sundries as per Cash Book. Individual lines go to the personal accounts: a debtor is credited with cash or bank received and with the discount allowed (**By Discount Allowed A/c**); a creditor is debited with the payment and the discount received (**To Discount Received A/c**).

sections.heading: 7. Overdraft and a definite cash balance
sections.body_md:
**Bank overdraft:** a credit balance of the bank column; the firm has paid out more through the bank than it deposited. An opening overdraft is **By Balance b/d** (credit side, bank column); a closing overdraft is **To Balance c/d** on the **debit** side and brought down on the credit side. A favourable bank balance is the reverse.

**Definite cash balance:** a firm may hold a fixed amount of cash at the close of each day, to limit cash on the premises, or at the end of a period. If cash is above the fixed amount, the **excess is deposited** in the bank (contra entry: bank column debited, cash column credited). If it is below, the **shortfall is withdrawn** from the bank (cash column debited, bank column credited). When the bank balance is smaller than the shortfall, the firm **avails an overdraft**, and the bank column then shows a credit balance.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**How marks are usually split (ISC Accounts)**
- 1 mark: one correct option, a term, or the side and column of one entry.
- 2 marks: a short explanation (why subsidiary books, what a contra entry is), or two entries such as a cheque kept and then deposited.
- 3 marks: a short cash book to balance (simple or triple column), the posting of one or two ledger accounts, or the treatment of cheques and discount.
- 5 marks: a full triple column cash book of about ten transactions, balanced, sometimes with the posting of the discount totals or of personal accounts.

**Step marks** usually go for the opening balances on the correct sides, the receipts and the payments in the correct columns, each contra entry on both sides, the discount columns, the balances carried down (cash, bank or overdraft) and the equal totals.

**Common mistakes**
- A receipt on the credit side, or By on the debit side.
- A deposit or withdrawal entered on one side only, or left unmarked.
- A kept cheque entered in the bank column, or a dishonoured cheque left in it.
- Balancing the discount columns, or posting the debit total to Discount Received A/c.
- Carrying an overdraft down on the credit side.
- A credit balance of cash left standing without rechecking the entries.

cards.front_md: **Subsidiary books**
cards.back_md: Books formed by dividing the journal so that each records one class of transactions.

cards.front_md: Why is the journal sub-divided?
cards.back_md: One journal cannot cope with the many similar transactions of a growing business; separate books share the work.

cards.front_md: Name two advantages of subsidiary books
cards.back_md: Division of work and saving of time (totals are posted); also specialisation, easy reference and an internal check.

cards.front_md: Which subsidiary book records cash received from a customer?
cards.back_md: The **cash book**.

cards.front_md: Which book records goods sent back to a supplier?
cards.back_md: The **purchases returns book**.

cards.front_md: Where does depreciation first get recorded?
cards.back_md: In the **journal proper**, which takes entries that fit no other book.

cards.front_md: **Cash book**
cards.back_md: The subsidiary book for all cash receipts and payments; it is also the Cash A/c, so no separate cash account is kept.

cards.front_md: Two roles of the cash book

cards.front_md: Which side takes receipts in the cash book?
cards.back_md: The **debit** side, with **To** and the other account.

cards.front_md: Which side takes payments in the cash book?
cards.back_md: The **credit** side, with **By** and the other account.

cards.front_md: Where does the opening cash balance go?
cards.back_md: First line on the debit side: **To Balance b/d**.

cards.front_md: Can cash in hand be a credit balance?
cards.back_md: **No.** A firm cannot pay out more cash than it holds; a credit balance signals a mistake.

cards.front_md: Balance c/d of the cash book: which side?
cards.back_md: The **credit** side, the smaller side; the b/d is then brought down on the debit side.

cards.back_md: Credit the debtor: **By Cash A/c** on the credit side of his account.

cards.front_md: Posting a payment to a creditor or an expense
cards.back_md: Debit the account: **To Cash A/c** on its debit side.

cards.front_md: Is a separate Cash A/c opened in the ledger?
cards.back_md: **No.** The cash book is itself the cash account.

questions.stem_md: Ojas Paints, an imagined wholesaler, finds that its single journal has grown too long for one clerk to write and check. It therefore splits the journal into separate books for cash, purchases, sales and returns. This sub-division mainly helps the firm to

options.text_md: avoid preparing a ledger altogether
share the recording among several clerks and total each book before posting
replace the trial balance by a summary of the books
make every kind of error impossible

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** share the recording among several clerks and total each book before posting. Each book handles one class of transactions, so different clerks can write them side by side and the totals of a book can be posted together. The ledger is still needed, the trial balance is still prepared, and clerical errors can still occur.

marking_scheme.step: Correct option (b)

cash book

questions.stem_md: What is meant by the sub-division of the journal? State the main reason for doing it.
questions.solution_md: Meaning, then the reason of growth in volume.

answer.model_answer_md:
It means splitting the single journal into several books, called **subsidiary books** or special journals, each meant for one class of transactions such as cash, credit purchases or credit sales.

The main reason is that in a growing business one journal cannot handle the large number of similar transactions, so the work is divided among books and clerks.

marking_scheme.step: Meaning: separate books for separate classes of transactions
Reason: volume of similar transactions, work divided among books and clerks

questions.stem_md: The owner of a growing trading firm is thinking of dividing the journal into subsidiary books. List two advantages she can expect, with a reason for each.
questions.solution_md: Any two of time saved, specialisation, easy reference, errors located, fraud checked.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Saving of time and labour:** a book contains like transactions, so only the total of a period need be posted to an account, instead of every item.
2. **Easy location of errors and information:** a clerk looks at one book to find a particular kind of transaction, and each clerk is answerable for his own book.

marking_scheme.step: First advantage with its reason
Second advantage with its reason

questions.stem_md: A trader who keeps a cash book writes cash receipts and payments in it directly, and does not open a separate Cash A/c in the ledger. This is possible because the cash book

options.text_md: records only those cash items that are not entered anywhere else
is written up from the journal at the end of every month
is a book of first entry and is also balanced like the Cash A/c
is kept for statistical purposes and has no accounting value

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** is a book of first entry and is also balanced like the Cash A/c. Transactions are entered in it first, and its two sides, receipts and payments, make it the cash account itself. It is not written up from the journal, it does not leave out items, and it is part of the formal books.

marking_scheme.step: Correct option (c)

questions.stem_md: The clerk of Harsh Optics, an imagined shop, totals the debit side of the simple cash book, opening cash included, as ₹39,800 and the credit side, before balancing, as ₹41,300. The right conclusion is that

options.text_md: a credit balance of ₹1,500 is carried down on the debit side
the firm has earned a profit of ₹1,500
there is an error, because cash paid out cannot exceed cash held, so the entries must be rechecked
the firm has taken an overdraft of ₹1,500 from its bank

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** there is an error, because cash paid out cannot exceed cash held, so the entries must be rechecked. A shop can pay out only the cash it has, so payments of 41,300 against 39,800 cannot both be right. A receipt was left out or a payment was entered wrongly. A credit balance in cash is not carried down, the excess of payments is not a profit, and a simple cash book has no bank column in which an overdraft could appear.

marking_scheme.step: Correct option (c)

questions.stem_md: Fatima Garments, an imagined shop, began a month with ₹12,000 in hand. Its cash receipts were ₹8,500 and ₹3,300 and its cash payments were ₹6,200 and ₹9,100. The balance carried down in the cash book is

marking_scheme.step: Correct option (a)

questions.solution_md: The cash book is both a journal for cash and the cash account.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. The cash book is a **book of original entry**: each cash receipt and payment is first recorded in it, in date order.
2. It is **balanced like a ledger account**, with receipts on the debit side and payments on the credit side, so it already serves as the Cash A/c and a second account would only repeat it.

questions.stem_md: After balancing, the cashier of Rohini Crafts, an imagined firm, finds that the credit side of the cash book exceeds the debit side by ₹1,200. Explain why this cannot be correct and name two likely causes.
questions.solution_md: Impossibility of a negative cash balance, then two causes.

answer.model_answer_md:
Cash in hand can never be a credit balance: the firm cannot pay out more cash than it held plus what it received. The difference shows a mistake.

Likely causes: (i) a **receipt was omitted** or posted to the wrong side; (ii) a **payment was entered twice** or with a larger amount than was paid.

marking_scheme.step: Reason: cash paid cannot exceed cash held
Two likely causes: omitted receipt, payment overstated or entered twice

options.text_md: discount, cash and bank
cash, bank and petty cash
debit, credit and balance
date, folio and amount

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** discount, cash and bank. A triple column cash book adds a bank column and a discount column to the cash column. Petty cash is kept in a separate book, and the other two sets are headings of other kinds of ruling.

questions.stem_md: Of the transactions of Varun Toys, an imagined shop, listed below, the one that is a contra entry is

options.text_md: payment of rent of ₹7,500 by cheque
withdrawal of ₹7,500 from the bank for use in the office
sale of goods for ₹7,500 in cash
allowing a discount of ₹7,500 to a customer

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** withdrawal of ₹7,500 from the bank for use in the office. A contra entry moves money between the cash column and the bank column, so the withdrawal stands on both sides of the same book. Rent by cheque touches the bank and a nominal account, cash sales touch cash and sales, and a discount touches a personal account.

marking_scheme.step: Correct option (b)

questions.stem_md: Hemant Rao, a customer, gave Madhav Electronics, an imagined shop, a cheque for ₹14,000 on 6 March, and the shop paid it into the bank on 9 March. In the cash book the entry made on 9 March is

options.text_md: a debit in the bank column, To Hemant Rao
a debit in the cash column, To Hemant Rao
a debit in the bank column, To Cash A/c, and a credit in the cash column, By Bank A/c, marked C
a credit in the bank column, By Hemant Rao

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** a debit in the bank column, To Cash A/c, and a credit in the cash column, By Bank A/c, marked C. On 6 March the cheque was entered in the cash column against Hemant Rao. Paying it in on 9 March only moves it from cash to bank, a contra entry on both sides. A second entry against the customer would count the same cheque twice.

marking_scheme.step: Correct option (c)

questions.stem_md: On 4 September Jaya Sports, an imagined shop, received a cheque for ₹9,500 from a debtor, Sohan Lal, after allowing him a discount of ₹500, and deposited it the same day. The entry in the cash book is

options.text_md: debit side: To Sohan Lal, discount ₹500, cash ₹9,500
credit side: By Sohan Lal, discount ₹500, bank ₹9,500
debit side: To Sohan Lal, bank ₹10,000, with no discount shown
debit side: To Sohan Lal, discount ₹500, bank ₹9,500

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** debit side: To Sohan Lal, discount ₹500, bank ₹9,500. A cheque paid in at once raises the bank balance, a receipt on the debit side, and the discount allowed is entered beside it in the debit discount column. The cash column is not touched, a credit entry would be a payment, and showing ₹10,000 in the bank would overstate the receipt.

marking_scheme.step: Correct option (d)

questions.stem_md: At the end of the month the discount column on the debit side of the cash book of Tushar Tyres, an imagined firm, totals ₹2,350 and the one on the credit side totals ₹1,100. The posting to the ledger is

options.text_md: credit Discount Allowed A/c with ₹2,350 and debit Discount Received A/c with ₹1,100
debit both discount accounts with ₹1,250
credit both discount accounts with ₹3,450
debit Discount Allowed A/c with ₹2,350 and credit Discount Received A/c with ₹1,100

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** debit Discount Allowed A/c with ₹2,350 and credit Discount Received A/c with ₹1,100. The debit column holds discounts allowed to customers, a loss of the firm, so it is posted as a debit to Discount Allowed. The credit column holds discounts received from suppliers, a gain, so it is a credit to Discount Received. The other options reverse the sides, or merge the two totals into ₹1,250 or ₹3,450, which loses the separate accounts.

marking_scheme.step: Correct option (d)

questions.stem_md: On 30 June, the balance of the bank column in the triple column cash book of Rohini Crafts, an imagined firm, is carried down on the debit side. This shows

options.text_md: a favourable balance at the bank
discount allowed to the debtors of the firm
an overdraft: the firm has paid out more through the bank than it paid in
cash in hand at the close of the month

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** an overdraft: the firm has paid out more through the bank than it paid in. A favourable bank balance is carried down on the credit side. When the balance goes on the debit side, the bank column has a credit balance, which means the bank has lent the difference. It has nothing to do with the discount or the cash column.

marking_scheme.step: Correct option (c)

questions.stem_md: A cheque for ₹7,000 received from Pooja Verma and deposited by Leela Textiles, an imagined firm, is returned unpaid by the bank. The entry in the cash book is

options.text_md: a debit in the bank column, To Pooja Verma
a credit in the bank column, By Pooja Verma
a credit in the cash column, By Pooja Verma
a debit in the discount column, To Pooja Verma

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** a credit in the bank column, By Pooja Verma. The bank balance of ₹7,000 that was added on deposit is taken back, a payment on the credit side of the bank column, and Pooja Verma is debited again in the ledger because she still owes the amount. A debit would repeat the receipt, and the cash column and the discount column are not involved.

marking_scheme.step: Correct option (b)

questions.stem_md: Which statement about the discount columns of a triple column cash book is correct?

options.text_md: They are only totalled, the two totals usually differ, and each is posted to its discount account
They are balanced like the cash column and the balance is carried down
They are posted to the personal accounts only and never to a discount account
They are not posted anywhere, because discount is not an accounting item

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** They are only totalled, the two totals usually differ, and each is posted to its discount account. The two discount totals are independent of each other and of the cash and bank columns, so there is no balance to carry down. Each total is posted once, while the individual items are posted to the personal accounts. Discount allowed and received are accounting items with accounts of their own.

marking_scheme.step: Correct option (a)

questions.stem_md: Dev Furniture, an imagined shop, received a customer's cheque on 12 May and paid it into the bank only on 15 May. Why is the cheque first entered in the cash column?

options.text_md: A cheque is always the same as cash in hand and never reaches the bank column
Until it is paid in, the firm holds the cheque and has no balance at the bank, so a contra entry is needed on deposit
The bank column is meant only for payments
The customer's account is not credited until the cheque is cleared

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Until it is paid in, the firm holds the cheque and has no balance at the bank, so a contra entry is needed on deposit. The bank column shows what the bank holds for the firm. A cheque kept in the drawer is held by the firm, so it joins the cash column, and the later deposit moves it across by a contra entry. The cheque does reach the bank column on deposit, the bank column also takes receipts, and the customer is credited when the cheque is received.

marking_scheme.step: Correct option (b)

options.text_md: avoid writing the cash column of the cash book
earn discount from the debtors of the firm
make the bank column show an overdraft
limit the cash exposed to theft on the premises while the rest stays safely at the bank

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** limit the cash exposed to theft on the premises while the rest stays safely at the bank. questions.solution_md: Fixed float; deposit of excess, withdrawal of shortfall.

answer.model_answer_md: The firm decides on a **fixed amount of cash** to hold at the close of each day. If the cash column shows more, the **excess is deposited** into the bank (cash column credited, bank column debited). If it shows less, the **shortfall is withdrawn** from the bank (cash column debited, bank column credited). Both are contra entries.

questions.stem_md: When a firm withdraws cash from the bank to make up its fixed cash balance but the bank balance is too small, what happens to the bank column? Explain with an example of your own.
questions.solution_md: Overdraft as a credit balance, with the example.

answer.model_answer_md: The withdrawal is allowed only if the bank has agreed to an **overdraft**, and the bank column then shows a **credit balance**. For example, with ₹2,000 at the bank and a shortfall of ₹4,500, the withdrawal of ₹4,500 leaves a credit balance of ₹2,500: an overdraft carried down on the debit side of the bank column.

marking_scheme.step: Overdraft arrangement needed; the bank column shows a credit balance
